title: Scientific Writing, Citations, and Using Credible Sources
text:
Student Pre-Lab Questions

What makes a question scientific?
Why must credible sources be used in biology?
What is a primary scientific source?
What is plagiarism?
When must a source be cited?
What is included in an in-text citation?
Which section explains why a study was conducted?

Overview
Biology is a scientific discipline grounded in observation, experimentation, and evidence-based reasoning. Scientific knowledge does not exist in isolation; it builds upon the work of other researchers. As a result, scientists must evaluate credible sources, cite prior work properly, and communicate findings clearly and accurately.
In this course, you will learn how to:

Ask scientific, testable questions
Identify and evaluate credible biological sources
Properly cite scientific literature
Communicate findings using accepted formats of scientific writing

Together, these skills form the foundation of scientific literacy and integrity.
Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, students will be able to:

Distinguish between scientific and non-scientific questions
Identify credible sources appropriate for biological research
Differentiate between primary, secondary, popular, and scholarly sources
Evaluate source credibility using objective criteria (CRAAP test)
Explain the importance of citation in scientific writing
Define plagiarism and identify examples of academic dishonesty
Apply proper in-text citation formats (APA or CSE style)
Describe the structure and purpose of sections in a scientific paper
Distinguish between Results and Discussion sections
Use writing practices that improve clarity, accuracy, and credibility

Scientific Questions and the Role of Evidence
Science focuses on questions that can be tested through observation, measurement, and experimentation.
Scientific Questions

Can be investigated empirically
Rely on measurable data
Are testable and repeatable


Examples:


What temperature maximizes bacterial growth?
Does a specific drug reduce disease symptoms?

Non-Scientific Questions

Cannot be tested using scientific methods
Often involve opinions, beliefs, or ethics


Examples:


What is the best genre of music?
Should cloning be allowed?

Only scientific questions can be addressed in laboratory investigations.
Using Credible Sources in Biology
Before conducting research, scientists review existing knowledge. Using credible sources ensures accuracy and reliability.
Types of Scientific Sources
Primary Sources

Original research articles
Present new data and experimental findings
Peer-reviewed and written by experts

Secondary Sources

Summarize or interpret primary research
Examples: textbooks, review articles

Popular vs. Scholarly Sources
The following table compares popular and scholarly sources, highlighting key differences in audience, review process, and reliability in scientific research.
Table 1. Comparison of Popular and Scholarly Sources in Scientific Research
This table compares popular and scholarly sources across several characteristics. Popular sources are written for a general audience, are not peer-reviewed, contain few or no citations, use simplified language, and include examples such as blogs and magazines. Scholarly sources are written for an expert audience, are peer-reviewed, include extensive references, use technical language, and include examples such as scientific journals like Science and Nature.



Popular Sources
Scholarly Sources




General audience
Expert audience


Not peer-reviewed
Peer-reviewed


Few or no citations
Extensive references


Simplified language
Technical language


Examples: blogs, magazines
Examples: Science, Nature



Scientific writing relies primarily on scholarly sources.
Evaluating Credibility: The CRAAP Test
To assess sources, use the CRAAP criteria:

Currency – Is the information recent?
Reliability – Is it from a trusted organization or journal?
Authority – Is the author qualified?
Accuracy – Is it supported by evidence?
Purpose – Is the content objective or biased?

Low-quality sources should not be used in scientific work.
Citing Sources and Avoiding Plagiarism
Why Citation Matters
Citations:

Distinguish your ideas from others
Credit original authors
Allow verification of information
Maintain academic integrity

What Is Plagiarism?
Plagiarism is presenting another person’s work as your own.
Examples:

Copying text without citation
Paraphrasing without credit
Submitting someone else’s work

Avoiding Plagiarism
Plagiarism is the act of presenting another person’s work, ideas, words, or creative output as your own without giving proper credit to the original source. This can include copying text directly, paraphrasing someone else’s ideas without acknowledgment, or submitting work that was created by someone else, such as a classmate or an online source. Plagiarism is considered a serious academic and ethical violation because it misrepresents authorship, undermines intellectual honesty, and deprives the original creator of recognition for their work.

Use your own words
Cite all non-original ideas
Keep accurate research notes
Use quotes sparingly in science

Citation Styles in Science
Scientific disciplines use standardized formats such as:

APA (Author–Year)
CSE (Name–Year commonly used in biology)

In-Text Citation Example

(Smith, 2020)

Reference List

Includes only sources cited in the paper
Organized alphabetically

Consistency in formatting is essential.
Writing for Science
Scientific writing emphasizes clarity, precision, and conciseness to ensure that ideas and findings are communicated effectively. Clarity means presenting information in a straightforward and understandable manner, avoiding ambiguity or unnecessary complexity. Precision involves using specific, accurate language and terminology so that the meaning is exact and scientifically correct. Conciseness requires eliminating unnecessary words or repetition, allowing the reader to quickly grasp the essential information without distraction. Together, these principles help make scientific communication efficient, credible, and accessible to other researchers.
Structure of a Scientific Paper
The structure of a scientific paper provides a standardized format that allows researchers to communicate findings clearly and logically. Each section has a specific purpose: the Introduction presents background and the research question, the Methods describe how the study was conducted, the Results report the data, and the Discussion interprets the findings. This organized approach helps readers quickly understand the study and evaluate its validity.
Title

Concise and descriptive

Abstract

Summary of purpose, methods, results, and conclusions
Written last

Introduction

Provides background and context
States research question or hypothesis
Explains importance of the study

Methods

Describes how the study was conducted
Allows replication
Includes materials and procedures

Results

Presents data and findings
Includes figures and tables
No interpretation

Discussion

Interprets results
Connects findings to existing research
Explains significance and limitations

Literature Cited

Lists all referenced sources

General Writing Practices

Be concise and precise
Use appropriate scientific terminology
Prefer active voice when appropriate
Use past tense for results, present tense for general knowledge
Avoid ambiguity and unnecessary detail
Treat “data” as plural
Italicize scientific names (Homo sapiens)
Revise and proofread carefully

Summary and Application to Laboratory Work
This chapter introduces the foundational skills required for success in biology, emphasizing the importance of scientific thinking, credible research, proper citation, and effective communication. Biology relies on evidence-based investigation, meaning that students must be able to ask testable scientific questions, evaluate reliable sources, and interpret data accurately. Understanding how to distinguish between scientific and non-scientific questions ensures that laboratory work remains focused on measurable and reproducible outcomes.
A key component of scientific work is the use of credible sources, particularly scholarly and peer-reviewed materials. Students learn to differentiate between primary and secondary sources and to evaluate credibility using criteria such as the CRAAP test. This ensures that conclusions are based on accurate, unbiased, and scientifically valid information.
Equally important is the ethical use of information. Proper citation practices allow students to give credit to original researchers, avoid plagiarism, and strengthen the credibility of their work. Using consistent citation formats such as APA or CSE helps maintain professional standards in scientific communication.
The chapter also introduces scientific writing, which prioritizes clarity, precision, and conciseness. Students learn the standard structure of a scientific paper—including Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion—and the purpose of each section. This structure ensures that experiments can be clearly understood, evaluated, and replicated.
Application to a Pre-Lab or Laboratory Report
In a pre-lab, students apply these skills by:

Formulating testable scientific questions or hypotheses
Researching background information using credible sources
Properly citing references used to justify the experiment

In a laboratory report, students:

Use the Introduction to explain the scientific question and support it with cited research
Describe procedures clearly in the Methods to allow replication
Present data objectively in the Results section
Interpret findings in the Discussion, connecting results to scientific literature
Include a properly formatted Literature Cited section

Overall, these skills ensure that laboratory work is not only accurate and ethical but also aligned with the standards of the scientific community.
Student Post-Lab Questions

How do citations improve scientific credibility?
What distinguishes scholarly from popular sources?
Give one example of plagiarism and explain why it is incorrect.
Why must Methods be replicable?
Why is interpretation excluded from Results?
How does Discussion differ from Results?
How do credible sources strengthen scientific conclusions?


Appendix: Scientific Writing, Citations, and Credible Sources Terms







Term
Definition




Abstract
A brief summary of a scientific paper including purpose, methods, results, and conclusions.


Accuracy
The correctness of information, supported by evidence and reliable sources.


APA Style
A citation format that uses author and date for referencing sources.


Authority
The credibility and qualifications of an author or source.


Bias
A tendency to present information in a non-objective or unfair way.


Citation
A reference to a source used to give credit and allow verification.


Clarity
The quality of being easy to understand in writing.


Conciseness
Expressing ideas clearly using as few words as necessary.


CRAAP Test
A tool used to evaluate sources based on Currency, Reliability, Authority, Accuracy, and Purpose.


Credible Source
A reliable and trustworthy source of information supported by evidence and expertise.


CSE Style
A citation format commonly used in biology that emphasizes author and year.


Discussion
A section of a scientific paper that interprets results and explains their significance.


Empirical
Based on observation or experiment rather than theory alone.


Introduction
The section of a paper that provides background and states the research question or hypothesis.


Literature Cited
A list of all sources referenced in a scientific paper.


Methods
The section describing how an experiment was conducted.


Peer Review
The evaluation of scientific work by experts before publication.


Plagiarism
Using another person’s work or ideas without giving proper credit.


Precision
Using exact and accurate language in scientific writing.


Primary Source
An original research article presenting new data.


Purpose
The intended goal or objective of a source or study.


Reliability
The consistency and dependability of a source.


Results
The section that presents data without interpretation.


Scholarly Source
A peer-reviewed source written for a scientific audience.


Scientific Question
A question that can be tested through observation and experimentation.


Secondary Source
A source that summarizes or interprets primary research.


Significance
The importance or meaning of findings in a scientific context.


Source Evaluation
The process of determining the credibility of a source.


Testable
Able to be examined through scientific experiment or observation.



Attribution Note
This chapter is adapted and synthesized from openly licensed instructional materials on scientific writing, citation practices, and evaluating sources, including OpenStax Biology and university library resources. Adapted for introductory biology laboratory instruction.

Overview of Pre-Lab Preparation
Preparing for your laboratory session is an important part of your success in this course. Before attending lab, you are expected to carefully review all assigned materials, including the lab manual, background readings, and any additional instructions provided by your instructor.
Effective reading requires active engagement. This means you should take your time, avoid skimming, and review the material more than once if necessary to fully understand the concepts and procedures. Thoughtful preparation will help you:

Work more efficiently during the lab
Make accurate observations
Better understand the purpose of the experiment

Important Note:
Not all instructors require a pre-lab assignment. Requirements may vary by faculty member, so it is your responsibility to check your course instructions or confirm expectations with your instructor before completing this work.

title: Pre-Lab Preparation and Responsible Use of AI
text:
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)
This course recognizes that students may use AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Copilot) to support learning. When used appropriately, AI can be helpful for:

Generating ideas or study questions
Clarifying difficult concepts
Improving grammar and writing clarity

However, AI is not a replacement for your own thinking or scientific understanding.

Key Expectations

AI is not a reliable scientific source
AI responses may be incorrect, incomplete, or misleading
You are responsible for verifying all information and completing your own work

AI Guidelines for This Lab

You are expected to:

Use AI only as a support tool, not as a source of answers

Take full responsibility for the accuracy of your work



You are not allowed to:

Submit AI-generated answers as your own work
Use AI instead of reading assigned lab materials

Section 1: Essential Ideas of the Lab
Identify the main scientific concept or procedure you will study.
Your response should address:
(a) What is already known about this topic? Include:

Key concepts and definitions
Important discoveries or developments
Any gaps or unanswered questions

(b) Why was this study performed?

Explain the purpose of the lab using the title and introduction

Requirements:

Write in your own words
Use credible sources (e.g., textbooks, lab manual)
Cite sources in APA format



Section 2: Lab Objectives
Describe what you will do during the lab.
Examples of objective actions:

Observe
Measure
Analyze
Determine

Requirements:

Use action-based statements (e.g., “To observe…”)
Focus on the procedures you will perform



Section 3: Purpose of the Lab
Explain how lab activities support your understanding of the scientific concept.
This section connects:

What you are doing
What you are learning

Requirement:

Clearly explain this relationship in your own words



Section 4: Hypothesis
(Required for experimental labs only: Labs 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9)
Develop a hypothesis (an educated prediction).
Steps:

Identify the independent variable (what you change)
Identify the dependent variable (what you measure)
Predict the relationship between them

Format:
If [independent variable changes], then [dependent variable will respond], because of [scientific reasoning].
Requirements:

Base your hypothesis on scientific knowledge
Clearly explain your reasoning
Cite any supporting information



Section 5: Questions
Write at least five thoughtful questions about the lab.
Your questions may focus on:

Concepts you find confusing
Steps in the procedure
Expected results



Section 6: References Cited
List all sources in APA (7th edition) format.

1.1 Introduction: Laboratory Safety and Measurement
Overall Laboratory Unit Objectives
Welcome to your first biology lab! Before you begin conducting experiments, it is essential to learn how to work safely and accurately in a laboratory setting. This lab will introduce you to the basic skills and habits that scientists use every day.
In the first part of this lab, you will learn about laboratory safety. Even in an introductory biology lab, there are potential hazards such as chemicals, glassware, biological materials, and heat sources. Understanding how to recognize these risks—and how to respond to them—helps protecting you, your classmates, and your experiments. Following safety rules also ensure that your results are reliable and free from contamination. These safety practices are not only important in class but are also essential in real-world careers such as healthcare, research, and biotechnology.
In the second part of this lab, you will focus on scientific measurement, which is a key skill in all areas of science. You will learn how to use the metric (SI) system, the standard system used by scientists worldwide. You will practice measuring length, mass, and volume using common laboratory tools such as rulers, balances, graduated cylinders, and pipettes. You will also learn how to convert between units, record data correctly, and organize your results.
Finally, you will explore how scientists evaluate data by learning the difference between accuracy (how close a measurement is to the true value) and precision (how consistent repeated measurements are). You will also practice calculating percent error and displaying your data using graphs.
Together, these skills—working safely, measuring carefully, and recording data accurately—form the foundation for all future lab work. Mastering them now will help you succeed in this course and prepare you for more advanced scientific investigations.

By the end of this laboratory unit, students will be able to:

Measurement and the Metric System
Learning Objectives
By the end of this lab, students will be able to:
Prelab Activity 1.1:
Students should complete these questions before coming to the lab.
Background:
Scientists use scientific methods to understand the natural world. An important aspect of the scientific process is collecting and analyzing data from observations and experiments. Two methods of measuring and recording data have been commonly used - the Imperial and the Metric System. The Imperial System uses units such as inches and pounds while the Metric System, a decimal-based system, uses units such as meters, liters, and grams. Because of its ease of use, the metric system is more widely used within the modern scientific community. The universal “language” of modern science is based on the metric system and learning to use it is the main purpose of this lab.
Part 1: Introduction to Metric System
Work conducted in science laboratories requires a functional understanding of the metric system, which serves as the standard system of measurement in scientific research. The metric system employs standardized, decimal-based units to measure length, mass, and volume, ensuring that measurements are precise, reproducible, and universally interpretable. Appropriate laboratory instruments are selected based on the quantity being measured; for example, balances are used to measure mass in grams, and graduated cylinders are used to measure liquid volume in milliliters.
The metric system is built upon a set of base units commonly used in biology. The meter (m) is the standard unit for measuring length; the liter (L) is used to measure volume, and the gram (g) is used to measure mass. Temperature in biological laboratories is typically measured in degrees Celsius (°C). All recorded measurements must include both a numerical value and the proper unit. For example, a measurement of 2 m indicates a length that is twice the base unit of length, the meter. Standard unit symbols and abbreviations are allowed and should be used consistently when recording data.
A primary advantage of the metric system is the ease with which units can be converted. Because the system is based on powers of ten, conversions involve multiplication or division by 10 or multiples of 10. For example, one decameter is equal to ten meters, and one kilometer is equal to one thousand meters. This base ten structure simplifies calculations, reduces the likelihood of errors, and makes the metric system especially well-suited for scientific measurements and laboratory applications.

Keep in mind each time you move the decimal point you are dividing by 10. When you are converting from a larger unit to a smaller, you will move the decimal point to the right. This means each time you move the decimal point you are multiplying by 10.

The fundamental unit of length in the metric system is the meter (m). In this laboratory exercise, length measurements will be made using centimeter (cm) rulers. As illustrated on a meter stick or metric ruler, one meter is equal to 100 centimeters (cm). When examining a metric ruler, each centimeter is subdivided into smaller intervals. Between each numbered centimeter marking, there are ten equally spaced hatch marks, each being one millimeter (mm). Therefore, ten millimeters are equal to one centimeter. Familiarity with these scale divisions is essential for accurately measuring and recording length in biological laboratory experiments.

Lab Activity 1.3: Taking Mass Measurements with an Electronic Balance
Weight measurements in science are also expressed in metric units. The basic unit is the gram (g). The electronic balances you will be using today are gram balances. The model you will be using will accurately measure 0.01 grams. There are 1000 grams in a kilogram. One of the most common units used in labs is the milligram (mg). There are 1000 milligrams in a gram. If you need a very small amount of something, you measure it in micrograms (µg). There are 106 µg in a gram. Some conversions are shown below:
1000 g = 1 kg
1 g = 1000 mg

Lab Activity 1.4: Volumetric Measurements
The metric unit for volume is the Liter (L). There are 1000 milliliters (mL) in one liter. Another common unit in volume is the microliter (µL). There are 106 µL in one liter and 1000 µL in one milliliter. Some common conversions are shown below:
1 L = 1000 mL
1 L = 1,000,000 µL (106 µL)
1 ml= 1000 µL (103 µL)
You will need to become familiar with the diverse types of instrumentation and glassware that you will be using throughout this semester. Today, we will focus on glassware and devices that measure larger volumes of liquid. You will also decide when a particular device is appropriate to use, based on the volume that you are dispensing. The types of measuring devices are quite different if you want to measure and dispense a liter versus a milliliter!

The volume of fluid in a graduated cylinder is measured by reading the bottom of the meniscus or the curved upper surface of the fluid in the graduated cylinder (red arrow)

These pipettes accurately dispense volumes of 1mL to 10mL and can be used for volumes up to 50 mL. You will be using mostly 1mL and 10mL serological pipettes in this class.
Reading a Meniscus
When measuring liquid volume in a pipette or graduated cylinder, it is important to read the meniscus, the curved surface of the liquid. Most liquids (like water) form a concave meniscus, meaning the surface curves downward.

Lab Activity 1.7: Accuracy and Precision
When making measurements, both precision and accuracy are extremely important. Precision of a measurement refers to the closeness of repeated measurements or the reproducibility of the measurement. Precision can be affected by the measuring instrument. If a student uses a thermometer calibrated to the nearest degree to measure the temperature of a beaker of water and a second student uses a thermometer that is calibrated to the nearest ten degrees for the same exercise, the reproducibility or precision of measurements will be greater for the student using the thermometer calibrated to the nearest degree. The thermometer with the greatest number of calibrations (smallest increments) is the most precise, and thus the reproducibility is greater. Accuracy, described as how close a measurement is to its true value, however, is dependent upon both the precision of the measuring instrument and the technical skills of the individual taking the measurement. You will perform an experiment to determine which instrument is most accurate and precise for measuring 10ml of liquid.

A. Laboratory Safety Knowledge


Identify common laboratory hazards like chemical, biological, physical, and equipment.
Explain the importance of laboratory safety in preventing injuries, ensuring valid results, and preparing for workplace environments.
Describe proper laboratory attire and personal protective equipment (PPE) and explain how each protects against specific hazards.


B. Laboratory Safety Skills


Demonstrate safe laboratory behaviors, including proper handling of materials, maintaining clean workspaces, and following instructions.
Apply correct emergency procedures, including responding to chemical spills and eye or skin exposure.
Properly dispose of laboratory waste, including glass, biological materials, and chemical substances.


C. Scientific Measurement Skills


Identify and use standard SI (metric) units for length, mass, volume, and temperature.
Perform accurate metric unit conversions using appropriate prefixes (kilo-, centi-, milli-, micro-).
Use laboratory instruments correctly, including rulers, balances, graduated cylinders, and pipettes.


D. Data and Scientific Reasoning


Record and report data accurately, including correct units, labels, and appropriate precision.
Differentiate between accuracy and precision and evaluate measurements based on these concepts.
Analyze measurement error and identify potential sources of error in laboratory procedures.


E. Professional and Scientific Practice


Demonstrate responsibility and accountability in a laboratory setting by following safety guidelines and maintaining appropriate conduct.
Explain how laboratory safety practices translate to real-world careers in healthcare, research, and biotechnology.






Prevents injuries such as burns, cuts, and exposure to harmful materials
Ensures accurate experimental results (no contamination or errors)
Builds professional habits required in healthcare, research, and laboratory jobs

Obtain a 100 mL beaker. This is the container you will use to weigh your water. It is not what you will use to measure in this experiment.
Place the beaker on the balance and tare it.
The target amount of water you will be measuring using a graduated cylinder is 42 mL. This has been recorded in Table 5.
Pour 42 mL of water into a 50 mL graduated cylinder. Be sure to read from the bottom of the meniscus.
Pour the 42 mL from the graduated cylinder into the tared beaker.
Determine the weight of the water and record as “Weight of Water.”
Convert this weight to mL. Water has a density of 1g/mL, therefore the number of g= number of mL (e.g. 50 g = 50 mL). Record this number as “Actual Volume Dispensed.”
Calculate the % error for each of your measurements as follows:



If you are not within an error range of +/- 5% then try again.
Note: Percent error is always reported as an absolute value, so no negative sign is included. For example, a calculated value of −5% is reported as 5% error.
